chunks: From the hadith of the atheist who questioned Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). Among his questions was that he said to him:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, but that is not in the manner found among creatures.'
That is because pleasure is a state that enters upon one, transferring one from one state to another, because the creature is hollow, active, and compound — things have an entry into it.
But our Creator — there is no entry for things into Him, because He is One, uniquely one in Essence, uniquely one in Concept.

So His pleasure is His reward, and His anger is His punishment — without any thing entering Him to provoke Him and transfer Him from one state to another, because that is among the attributes of the creatures who are incapable and needy.

key_terms.أجوف: Ajwaf — hollow, empty inside; used to characterize the internal receptivity of created beings
key_terms.الرضا: Al-Rida — divine pleasure or approval; here distinguished from its creaturely form
key_terms.الزنديق: Zindiq — atheist, freethinker, or materialist; in early Islamic parlance, one who denies the truth of religion
key_terms.السخط: Al-Sakhat — divine anger or wrath; likewise distinguished from creaturely emotion
key_terms.مركب: Murakkab — compound, composite; having multiple parts that interact
key_terms.معتمل: Mu'tamil — active, in motion, operative; denotes a being whose parts work upon each other
key_terms.واحدي الذات: Wahidi al-Dhat — uniquely/absolutely one in Essence, a technical theological term for God's indivisible simplicity
key_terms.واحدي المعنى: Wahidi al-Ma'na — uniquely one in Concept/Meaning, denoting God's semantic unity

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about God's pleasure and anger compared to those of created beings?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) responds to a questioning atheist's challenge about whether God possesses pleasure and anger, affirming these divine attributes while categorically denying they operate as they do in creatures. He explains that creaturely emotions are states that 'enter' a being and alter it, because creatures are hollow, compound, and permeable. God, being absolutely One in Essence and Concept, admits no such external influence; His pleasure and anger are simply His reward and punishment — functional descriptions of His actions rather than emotional transformations. The theological context was the vibrant intellectual debates of 8th-century Kufa, where Hisham ibn al-Hakam and other Shia theologians engaged materialists and freethinkers with rational arguments.
